articles.title: Justin Martinez throws D-backs' second immaculate inning of the season
articles.summary: An immaculate inning (a nine-pitch, three-strikeout inning) is a more rare achievement than a no-hitter.
articles.body:
Justin Martinez was immaculate on Friday.

To be more specific, the Arizona Diamondbacks reliever threw an immaculate inning against the Texas Rangers , striking out three hitters on three pitches each in the sixth frame. Six of those pitchers were faster than 100 mph.

With only 123 immaculate innings in MLB history, it remains a feat more rare than a no-hitter, though there have been far more in recent years as pitchers dial up their velocity and throw fewer complete games.

It is also the second immaculate inning for the D-backs this season, as Michael Soroka threw one in the fourth game of their season on March 30 against the Detroit Tigers . There have been two others in MLB this season, by Gavin Williams of the Cleveland Guardians (July 23) and Taj Bradley of the Minnesota Twins (Aug. 25).

Martinez is in his fourth season with the D-backs and made his return from Tommy John surgery last month. He hasn't allowed a run in eight appearances since, while striking out 11 and allowing only two hits in 7 2/3 innings.

images.caption: Justin Martinez's return from Tommy John surgery is going pretty well. (Christian Petersen via Getty Images)

articles.title: Every MLB Team's Worst Bang-For-Your-Buck Player in 2026
articles.summary: A lot of Major League Baseball players are worth every penny of their salary and then some, but there are also an awful lot of highly paid players who have not been productive in 2026.
articles.body:
A lot of Major League Baseball players are worth every penny of their salary and then some, but there are also an awful lot of highly paid players who have not been productive in 2026.

In fact, every team has at least one player who definitively has not lived up to his salary. (Including players who have missed the entire season due to injury. They're still getting paid, after all.)

Let it be known that the monetary data points we are using today are luxury tax salaries, per Spotrac .

Using Shohei Ohtani's preposterously deferred 10-year, $700M contract as an example, his AAV is $70M and he is presently receiving $2M cash per year, but for the Dodgers' luxury tax purposes, he counts as $46.1M. We're interested in that latter figure for this exercise. (Though, Ohtani is nowhere close to LAD's LVP, to be clear.)

The following 30 players have a cumulative tax salary of $663.2 million and have been worth a combined 0.9 wins below replacement.

Statistics are current through the start of play on Friday.

Baltimore Orioles : RHP Chris Bassitt, $18.5M 2026 Stats: 85.1 IP, 4.96 ERA, 1.58 WHIP, 6.4 K/9, 0.4 bWAR

Between Craig Kimbrel ($13M) in 2024, Charlie Morton ($15M) last year and now Chris Bassitt, the Orioles will probably think twice this offseason before signing another late-in-his-career pitcher to an eight-figure deal. In Bassitt's defense, he did have a solid three-year run with Toronto, both in terms of durability and production. But both his cutter and his four-seamer have devolved into batting-practice pitches. His strikeout rate has plummeted to 15.7 percent after five consecutive years north of 22.

Boston Red Sox : LHP Garrett Crochet, $28.3M 2026 Stats: 30.0 IP, 6.30 ERA, 1.47 WHIP, 11.1 K/9, -0.5 bWAR

Crochet was nothing short of fantastic for the Red Sox in 2025, leading the majors in strikeouts while finishing second in the AL Cy Young vote. If they hadn't already signed him to a six-year, $170M deal one week into last season, it surely would've cost even more to lock him up long-term this past winter. Unfortunately, in the first year of that contract, he made three quality starts, two subpar starts and one horrific start before hitting the shelf in late April. (They're still hoping he can pitch in relief in October, but we'll see.)

New York Yankees : DH Giancarlo Stanton, $22M 2026 Stats: .256/.302/.422, 3 HR, 14 RBI, 24 games, 0.2 bWAR

Stanton missing a significant chunk of the season to recover from an injury has been an annual rite of passage for eight years at this point. He usually plays enough to still make an impact, averaging 108.2 games played and 28.2 home runs over the previous five seasons. No such luck this year; he last appeared in a game on April 24 due to calf injuries. Even while healthy, he was a league-average hitter with a 100 OPS+.

Tampa Bay Rays : LHP Steven Matz, $7.5M 2026 Stats: 74.0 IP, 5.72 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 6.6 K/9, -0.9 bWAR

Acquiring Gavin Lux's $5.525M salary in January and then having him miss the entire season (thus far, at least) with shoulder and ankle injuries was a rare whiff from the Rays. But at least he's costing them $2M less than Matz and isn't actively hurting the team with what has been one of the worst ERAs among MLB pitchers who have logged at least 70 innings in 2026. Even since transitioning to the bullpen in early June, Matz has allowed multiple runs in nearly one-third of his appearances.

Toronto Blue Jays : RHP José Berríos, $18.7M 2026 Stats: N/A

Cases certainly could be made for Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and/or George Springer here, as those co-faces of the franchise haven't exactly carried their weight for a combined luxury tax hit of more than $60M. At least they're playing and providing some positive value, while both Berríos and Anthony Santander ($14.7M) have been complete sunk costs. Berríos might miss all of 2027, too, as he didn't undergo Tommy John surgery until late May.

Chicago White Sox : DH Andrew Benintendi, $15M 2026 Stats: .242/.304/.421, 14 HR, 70 RBI, 0.2 bWAR

In season No. 4 of Benintendi's five-year, $75M contract, it's hardly breaking news that he isn't living up to the billing. He had a 2.9 bWAR in 2021 and another 2.9 mark in 2022, but he has been worth a cumulative 0.6 wins above replacement since. At least he's rarely playing the field this year, though, because Benintendi's value "added" in left field over the previous three seasons was equal to Nick Castellanos' impact in right field.

Cleveland Guardians : RHP Shawn Armstrong, $5.5M 2026 Stats: 33.0 IP, 4.91 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 9.0 K/9, 0.0 bWAR

Considering José Ramírez made up more than 25 percent of Cleveland's Opening Day payroll, he is making more than twice what his closest teammate is making and is having his worst season in more than a decade. You could make a compelling argument for him in this spot. However, even "worse than usual" Ramírez is still one of the more valuable players on the Guardians roster, while Armstrong has given them nothing in return for the fourth-highest salary on the team.

Detroit Tigers : LHP Framber Valdez, $36.6M 2026 Stats: 157.2 IP, 4.17 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 6.8 K/9, 1.2 bWAR

From a purely "value added per dollar received" perspective, the correct answer for Detroit would be Javier Báez, worth a negative 0.7 bWAR for a $23.3M tax salary. However, when the Tigers gave Valdez $115M in early February, they immediately became one of the top threats to reach the World Series. It is largely because of a 12-16 record in his turns through the rotation and a worst-by-far-in-his-career strikeout rate that the Tigers have fallen a mile short of expectations.

Kansas City Royals : RHP Seth Lugo, $23M 2026 Stats: 159.0 IP, 5.04 ERA, 1.44 WHIP, 6.7 K/9, -0.3 bWAR

With a 1.15 ERA through his first five starts, Lugo was one of the precious few things about this team that wasn't a mess early on. Since that promising start, however, Lugo has made 24 starts with a 5.99 ERA, allowing more hits and runs than any other pitcher in baseball since April 21. He was one of the biggest reasons Kansas City made the playoffs in 2024. Now, he's one of the biggest reasons the Royals are jockeying for draft lottery odds.

Minnesota Twins : RHP Pablo López, $18.4M 2026 Stats: N/A

Hate to put a guy on this list who suffered a season-ending injury about five seconds into spring training. But aside from the money Minnesota retained in the Carlos Correa trade, López and Byron Buxton ($14.3M) are the only players the Twins are paying more than $7M this season. If López hadn't gotten hurt, there's a decent chance the Twins would be leading the AL Central right now.

Athletics : RHP Luis Severino, $22.3M 2026 Stats: 62.2 IP, 4.16 ERA, 1.47 WHIP, 9.3 K/9, 0.9 bWAR

Severino's numbers aren't bad compared to most of the A's pitching staff, but he also hasn't pitched since May, missing out on the warm summer months at Sutter Health Park, where fly balls carry like the pre-humid days at Coors Field. Plus, for darn near triple the salary of the next-highest-paid pitcher on the team, the A's were hoping he would be better than "comparatively not bad." They were also hoping he would make more than 12 starts.

Houston Astros : 2B Jose Altuve, $25M 2026 Stats: .246/.309/.400, 15 HR, 44 RBI, 0.1 bWAR

If we could roll up Lance McCullers Jr., Cristian Javier and Tatsuya Imai into one big, $47.8M sandwich of pitching disappointment, that'd be a great pick here. It's frankly a miracle that Houston is in a position to make the postseason in spite of darn near the worst starting rotation in baseball. But Altuve still making bank while struggling to remain anything more than a replacement-level player is a major hurdle the Astros have needed to clear both this season and last. (And he still has three years left on his contract.)

Los Angeles Angels : 3B Anthony Rendon, $35.6M 2026 Stats: N/A

The Angels and Rendon agreed to restructure the contract this past offseason so that his 2026 salary gets deferred to 2028-30. He still counts against the 2026 luxury tax payroll, giving us one more chance to revisit one of the worst contracts in MLB history. Rendon was solid in 2020, but he has a .666 OPS and a cumulative 1.7 bWAR in the six seasons since, playing in just 205 games.

Seattle Mariners : RHP Luis Castillo, $21.6M 2026 Stats (with Seattle): 99.2 IP, 5.06 ERA, 1.40 WHIP, 7.8 K/9, -0.7 bWAR

If you were expecting Cal Raleigh here, you've slept through the part where he has a 1.200 OPS over his last 18 games. His resurgence has done nothing to help salvage Seattle's dreadful record, but at least he has turned things around. Castillo never did, and it's a small miracle that the M's managed to trade him (and what's left on his contract) to Chicago ahead of the deadline.

Texas Rangers : SS Corey Seager, $32.5M 2026 Stats: .227/.322/.430, 17 HR, 40 RBI, 2.7 bWAR

Despite a sub-.500 record, Texas doesn't have an obvious candidate for this list. The five Rangers making big bucks have each been worth better than one win above replacement. But Seager is sort of the poster boy of a Rangers team that has been banged up and not as productive as usual. He does have a .954 OPS over his last 26 games played, but he was batting .192 through Texas' first 120 games, missing 59 of them.

Atlanta Braves : SS Ha-Seong Kim, $20M 2026 Stats: .126/.211/.136, 0 HR, 8 RBI, 2 SB, -0.6 bWAR

As bad as those numbers are, they were even worse before Kim went 3-for-3 on Sept. 1 and followed it up with his first extra-base hit of the season (a hustle double on a slow line drive) the following day. He has dealt with multiple significant injuries over the past two years, but it's hard to believe this is the same guy who racked up 28 home runs and 60 stolen bases between the 2023 and 2024 campaigns in San Diego.

Miami Marlins : RHP Pete Fairbanks, $13M 2026 Stats: 40.1 IP, 6.02 ERA, 1.31 WHIP, 12.7 K/9, -1.1 bWAR

From 2023-25, Fairbanks was one of 12 pitchers to record at least 75 saves, and one of just six to do so with a sub-3.00 ERA. But that success in Tampa did not follow him to Miami. Heck, he didn't even have a month in 2026 with a sub-3.00 ERA. And though he has 18 saves, he's also had seven instances where he either blew a save or suffered the loss. If the Marlins had just run it back again with Calvin Faucher as their primary closer, they might have been right there with San Diego and Arizona for the last wild card spot.

New York Mets : DH Jorge Polanco, $20M 2026 Stats: .148/.201/.230, 2 HR, 6 RBI, -1.4 bWAR

There are more expensive Mets who simply haven't delivered the goods, including Marcus Semien ($24M), Francisco Lindor ($34.1M), Bo Bichette ($42M) and even Juan Soto ($51.1M). Polanco remains the crux of everything that went wrong for New York over the past 10 months, never even making a formal offer to Pete Alonso and then deciding to throw $40M at a guy who had never previously played first base in his MLB career.

Philadelphia Phillies : SS Trea Turner, $27.3M 2026 Stats: .241/.293/.388, 19 HR, 56 RBI, 19 SB, -0.2 bWAR

Turner entered 2026 as a career .297 hitter, but he has been unable to keep his on-base percentage—let alone his batting average—at that mark this year. After a great 2025 in the field, his defense has taken a colossal step backward with an MLB-worst 21 errors. Though it's a near certainty he'll join the 20/20 club for the fourth time in his career, it also might be one of the five least valuable 20/20 campaigns in MLB history.

Washington Nationals : RHP Stephen Strasburg, $35M 2026 Stats: N/A

If we're including the final year of Rendon's seven-year, $245M nightmare of a contract, we've got to do the same with Strasburg. (And thank goodness, because the Nationals otherwise don't have a single 2026 luxury tax salary north of $7M.) Strasburg hasn't pitched since 2022, retiring from baseball in 2024. He had a 6.89 ERA in the eight appearances he was able to make during this ill-fated deal.

Chicago Cubs : RHP Jameson Taillon, $17M 2026 Stats (with Chicago): 76.0 IP, 5.92 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 8.1 K/9, -1.0 bWAR

Had he been able to make a full 32-33 starts, Taillon would have been on track to become the first pitcher in MLB history to allow more than 50 home runs in a single season. By some miracle, the Cubs convinced the Blue Jays to absorb nearly one-third of this salary ahead of the trade deadline, after they designated him for assignment in late July with a bunch of career-worst numbers on his stat sheet.

Cincinnati Reds : DH/3B Eugenio Suárez, $15M 2026 Stats: .208/.302/.421, 22 HR, 63 RBI, 0.1 bWAR

Suárez was supposed to be Cincinnati's solution to not having a legitimate slugger or a go-to choice at DH in 2025. And though he has heated up over the past six weeks, the Reds couldn't even give him away at the trade deadline with a .663 OPS at the time. Because he hasn't delivered the way they hoped he would—and because the likes of TJ Friedl, Matt McLain, Ke'Bryan Hayes and Noelvi Marté have been so much worse—Cincinnati is currently the National League's lowest scoring team.

Milwaukee Brewers : RHP Brandon Woodruff, $22.025M 2026 Stats: 45.1 IP, 2.98 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 9.3 K/9, 1.0 bWAR

Woodruff was dominant while healthy. However, for the fourth consecutive year, he made 12 or fewer starts, making the "while healthy" portion of his season far too short. Let's not forget: Woodruff also got a $10M payout from the $20M mutual option that he declined in November, so they effectively paid him $32.025M for roughly one quarter of a season. (They're still on track to set a franchise record for wins in a season, though. Madness.)

Pittsburgh Pirates : DH Marcell Ozuna, $12M 2026 Stats: .203/.286/.327, 8 HR, 29 RBI, -1.1 bWAR

Two years removed from finishing fourth in the 2024 NL MVP vote, Ozuna would make a compelling case for top five in this year's NL Least Valuable Player vote, if there were such a thing. His OPS went from .925 in 2024 to .756 in 2025, all the way down to .612 this year before the Pirates finally threw in the towel. Toward the end, they even tried deploying him almost exclusively against left-handed pitchers, but it didn't help.

St. Louis Cardinals : OF Lars Nootbaar, $5.25M 2026 Stats (with St. Louis): .234/.333/.354, 3 HR, 16 RBI, 0.2 bWAR

The Cardinals don't have any good candidates here, as they sold off most of their expensive pieces during the offseason. Only Nootbaar and Dustin May had salaries of at least $5M. May had an impressive 3.14 FIP before they traded him to Milwaukee. But Nootbaar missed the first two months of the season and had a .521 OPS over his final 25 games before getting traded to Arizona.

Arizona Diamondbacks : RHP Corbin Burnes, $32.9M 2026 Stats: 3.0 IP, 0.00 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 6.0 K/9, 0.2 bWAR

He's finally back from Tommy John surgery, and not a moment too soon. Burnes made his 2026 debut on Tuesday, tossing three scoreless innings against the Royals. With any luck, he'll be stretched out enough to go six or seven innings during the do-or-die final weekend of the regular season against the San Diego Padres, possibly again during the wild card round. If that happens and he helps get the Diamondbacks into the NLDS, the lengthy rehab will have been worth every penny. For now, though, those three innings sure have cost a lot of money.

Colorado Rockies : OF Kris Bryant, $26M 2026 Stats: N/A

It'll never quite approach Rendon/Strasburg levels of disaster, simply because Bryant's $182M contract isn't even 75 percent as expensive as those $245M swings and misses. But since the beginning of 2023, Bryant has played in 128 games with a .642 OPS and a negative-2.3 bWAR . At this point, he's frankly helping the Rockies by simply cashing his checks while not picking up a bat.

Los Angeles Dodgers : OF Kyle Tucker, $57.2M 2026 Stats: .225/.323/.361, 13 HR, 60 RBI, 10 SB, 0.3 bWAR

We previously mentioned Marcell Ozuna's year-over-year fall from OPS grace since 2024. Well, Tucker is right there with him, going from a .993 OPS in 2024 to an .841 mark last year, down to the current eyesore of .684. The Dodgers would have to be thrilled if he could start even producing at that level as of late, but he has triple-slashed .143/.255/.242 over his last 27 games. If that doesn't change and if Andy Pages makes it back in time for the postseason, Tucker might be a $57.2M benchwarmer in October.

San Diego Padres : RHP Joe Musgrove, $20M 2026 Stats: N/A

Neither Manny Machado nor Xander Bogaerts has lived up to their exorbitant salaries this season, but at least they're both putting in reps, missing a combined total of seven games this season. Musgrove, on the other hand, has suffered one setback after another from the Tommy John surgery he had 23 months ago. He didn't pitch at all in 2025. It's not looking promising that he'll make it back onto a big-league mound in 2026.

San Francisco Giants : RHP Tyler Mahle, $10M 2026 Stats (with San Francisco): 94.2 IP, 5.13 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 8.5 K/9, -0.2 bWAR

Mahle is one of 10 players who opened the season on the Giants roster with a tax salary of at least $10M. Most of those players failed to live up to their potential. But Mahle, in particular, has to be a point of frustration for Giants fans, blossoming into an ace the instant they traded him away, boasting a 1.24 ERA in six starts with Atlanta. It would be one final kick in the teeth for San Francisco if Mahle ends up imploding in the NLDS to help the Dodgers advance.

articles.title: Notes: MLB expansion, position players pitching, 2028 Olympics
articles.summary: One aspect of the upcoming labor battle this offseason, after the collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, is Major League Baseballs desire to...
articles.body:
One aspect of the upcoming labor battle this offseason, after the collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, is Major League Baseballs desire to expand from 30 to 32 teams.

MLB's last expansion was in 1998, and Jeff Passan at ESPN in his outline of potential new cities notes that commissioner Rob Manfred wants the league to decide on one west coast and one east coast team by January 2029.

It will be at least three decades before MLB adds more teams, the longest stretch without expansion since the first 60 years of the American League (1901-60) saw eight teams in each league for a total of 16 teams. Since then:

1961: 16 to 18 teams (Angels, new Senators added)

1969: 20 to 24 (Expos, Padres, Royals, Seattle Pilots)

1977: 24 to 26: ( Blue Jays , Mariners )

Matt Brown expertly covers the business of college sports at his Extra Points newsletter, and analyzed how the potential MLB expansion cities might affect revenue for some college programs .

Sam Miller at his Pebble Hunting newsletter isn't a fan of the trend of more position players pitching:

It's a bit surprising to me that baseball, which has so many unwritten rules about what players should and shouldn't do when the game is out of hand, has settled on such a bizarre, asymmetrical surrender when it comes to position players pitching. The pitcher throws the single worst pitch he can. The batter then takes a massive overswing.

Bill Shaikin at the Los Angeles Times argues that Major League Baseball, the Players Association, and LA28 should figure out a way to come to an agreement on making MLB players available to play in the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles:

The league says play ball, but not without the authority to punish players that do not wish to play. The union says play ball, but not unless the league eases up on mandatory participation, and unless LA28, the international baseball federation and the International Olympic Committee provides major league players with flexibility in areas such as accommodations, tickets and marketing rights.

However, the game was briefly interrupted when a spectator carrying a Palestinian flag ran from the stands onto the field. Yankee Stadium security quickly tackled the man. He reportedly timed the field invasion at exactly 9:11 p.m. Details about how the person reached the field were not immediately clear. articles.title: Brewers clinch playoffs, become first team in MLB history to record multiple shutout wins of 20-plus runs in a season
articles.summary: Milwaukee pulverized the Cincinnati Reds on Friday night at home.
articles.body:
What the Brewers accomplished on Friday night somehow rivaled that head-turning performance. At Milwaukee's American Family Field, they once again authored utter domination, this time versus the Cincinnati Reds .

With a 20-0 shellacking of the Reds (69-78), the Brewers (92-56) clinched a playoff berth. Plus, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs, Milwaukee became the first team in MLB history to record multiple shutout wins of 20-plus runs in a season , and it accounted for the largest victory by any team on the day it clinched a postseason spot .

The Brewers have now made the playoffs eight of the past nine seasons. That batch of postseason appearances includes the 2023 season, during which they punched their ticket to October baseball with a 15-run road win over the Miami Marlins .

So they're used to entering the bracket with some oomph. The question remains, can Milwaukee translate its regular-season success into a World Series run?

After all, the Brewers have made it there only once, and that was in 1982, when they were part of the American League and lost to the St. Louis Cardinals in seven games. They've since reached the NLCS three times, including twice during this illustrious nine-season span.

Over the course of the season, it's been reasonable to ask if the Brewers have enough power to charge, at the very least, a long-awaited push for the NL pennant. They rank second to last in the majors in home runs this season .

On Friday, though, the Brewers hit four homers, including their first grand slam of the year. That four-run special was clobbered by outfielder Garrett Mitchell . Second baseman Brice Turang went yard, too, and enjoyed a 3-for-3 day, also nabbing four RBI.

Catcher William Contreras led the team with six RBI. His homer was the last of the round-trippers, and it delivered a trio of runs in the eighth inning. By then, the six innings of shutout ball Brewers righty Dustin May hurled looked that much more impressive.

Milwaukee has the best record in baseball and two of the most convincing wins in recent memory. The playoffs await the NL Central-leading Brewers.

articles.title: Dodgers are first MLB team with 90 wins in 13 full seasons in a row
articles.summary: Friday’s victory over the Miami Marlins was the Dodgers’ 90th win of the season, a mark that has long been seen as a sign of success in baseball and has amaz...
articles.body:
Friday's victory over the Miami Marlins was the Dodgers' 90th win of the season, a mark that has long been seen as a sign of success in baseball and has amazingly become the floor for the Dodgers for 14 years running.

The Dodgers have won at least 90 games in each of the last 13 full seasons, dating back to 2013. During the truncated 2020 campaign the Dodgers were 43-17, which was the best record in baseball. Thirteen full seasons in a row with 90 wins is more than any other MLB team in history.

From 1947-58 the New York Yankees won at least 92 games every year for a dozen years in a row, a streak even more impressive because it was under a 154-game schedule instead of the modern 162. The 1946 Yankees won 87 games, the equivalent of 91.5 wins over 162 games, so it's far to say these current Dodgers are at least spiritually even with those dominant Yankees teams.

The Yankees from 1946-58 had a .626 winning percentage, 29 points ahead of the next-best team during that time (Brooklyn at .597). Since 2013, the Dodgers have a .610 win percentage, 46 points ahead of the next-best team , the Yankees at .564.

There's no question the Dodgers' financial largesse has made it easier for them to compete , but money doesn't always guarantee winning. The New York Mets , for instance, have spend well over $300 million last season and this year with no postseason to show for it. The Yankees, who have spent the second-most behind the Dodgers since 2013, have won 90 games seven times in that span, and will add an eighth 90-win season with only five more victories this year.

That's still five full seasons for the Yankees with under 90 wins during that time, despite the heavy spending.

Cleveland is the only other team with even seven 90-win seasons since 2013. The Houston Astros , Milwaukee Brewers , and St. Louis Cardinals have six such seasons, including this year for Milwaukee. The Atlanta Braves , Chicago Cubs , and Milwaukee Brewers have five such seasons with an excellent chance to also win 90 games this year.

But to win 90 games in all 13 full seasons is a remarkable accomplishment, no matter how you slice it.

To put in further perspective, prior to this streak of 13 full seasons in a row with at least 90 wins, the Dodgers won 90 games 18 times in their first 55 seasons in Los Angeles , roughly once every three years.

articles.title: Gerrit Cole's Box Score Stats, Reaction from Rough Yankees vs. Mets Outing amid Continued Struggles
articles.summary: New York Yankees starting pitcher Gerrit Cole has now allowed seven home runs over his last two starts after a rough outing against the New York Mets on Saturday afternoon.
articles.body:
New York Yankees starting pitcher Gerrit Cole has now allowed seven home runs over his last two starts after a rough outing against the New York Mets on Saturday afternoon.

The Mets hit homers in the first, second and third innings courtesy of shortstop Francisco Lindor, Luis Torrens and Carson Benge, respectively. Lindor and Benge hit solo shots, while Torrens smacked a two-run, two-out homer.

Predicting Every Team's Opening Day Lineup 🔮

Cole got into trouble in the fifth, allowing an RBI double to Benge to put the Yankees in a 5-1 hole, and was swiftly yanked by manager Aaron Boone.

Last Sunday against the San Diego Padres, Cole began his start by allowing back-to-back-to-back home runs to Fernando Tatis Jr., Jake Cronenworth and Manny Machado. He later gave up a solo homer to Jorge Campusano in the seventh inning en route to a 4-3 loss.

All told, Cole gave up these seven homers in a span of 9.1 innings pitched.

The 36-year-old Cole is a six-time All-Star, two-time American League ERA leader and one-time AL Cy Young winner (2023). He missed all of 2025 after undergoing Tommy John surgery and returned on May 22.

Cole got his season off to a great start, throwing 12.2 shutout innings over a pair of starts against the Tampa Bay Rays and Kansas City Royals.

However, it's been an up-and-down campaign ever since.

Cole endured a tough nine-game stretch in which he allowed 11 home runs en route to a 4.93 ERA.

He fared a lot better over his next six starts (1.96 ERA) while allowing just two home runs and striking out 39 batters (vs. just nine walks).

September has been a rough go, though. Cole first labored through a start against the last-place Los Angeles Angels, allowing three earned runs and eight hits in 5.1 innings. Now he's struggled mightily against the Padres and Mets, who have done quite well against Cole as a Yankee.

Cole's next turn in the rotation is set for Friday at the Arizona Diamondbacks.

articles.title: MLB standings 2026: Updated playoff bracket, magic numbers through Sept. 12
articles.summary: The chase for October is on. Follow along with the updated MLB standings, playoff bracket and magic numbers.
articles.body:
It will still take some time for the leaves to change colors, but the chase for October is upon us.

The MLB postseason, which actually begins in late September, will be framed as a battle between David and Goliath, with 11 Davids and one Goliath: the Los Angeles Dodgers .

While the Dodgers haven't looked unbeatable in the regular season, they have positioned themselves as the villains after following back-to-back championships with the trade deadline acquisition of Tarik Skubal.

Everyone else, whether in a big market or a small market, will enter the postseason as some degree of an underdog. After the Blue Jays nearly dethroned the Dodgers last fall, could 2026 be the year a different team climbs to the top?

Here's an updated look at the MLB standings, including who's in and who's out for October.

Standings updated through games on Sept. 12.

* Indicates clinched postseason berth ** Indicates clinched division title *** Indicates clinched first-round bye

Some teams have spent most of 2026 knowing that reaching the postseason was a near certainty, but officially clinching a bid is still a massive moment of relief for both the organization and the fans.

12 teams will clinch a postseason berth by the end of the day on Sept. 27, and the last handful of spots could come down to the final weekend. Magic numbers are one way to tell how close each team is to clinching.

The math behind magic numbers is as follows: Add one team's wins and the losses of the trailing team, then subtract it from 163. If a team leading the division has 90 wins and the second-place team has 63 losses, their magic number would sit at 10. Because tiebreaker games no longer occur, though, the magic number can be one number higher or lower based on which team owns the head-to-head tiebreaker.

The first number below is the magic number for teams leading the division or wild-card races to clinch that race. The second number is the elimination number for teams trailing the division or wild-card races, and how far they are from division or playoff elimination. Two x's means a team has been eliminated from that race or has won it.

articles.title: Each MLB Team's Nightmare Scenario Down the Stretch of 2026 Season
articles.summary: Major League Baseball's regular season is a marathon, and with just two weeks to go, the race is almost over.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball's regular season is a marathon, and with just two weeks to go, the race is almost over.

Who is going to embarrassingly collapse just before the finish line?

We promise not to waste your time with "star player suffers big injury" nor "team loses every single game left on its schedule" nightmare scenarios. Everyone already knows those are the worst possible outcomes.

However, prepare yourself for quite a few "sputters to the finish line and misses the postseason" potential nightmares, as there are still 10 teams realistically jockeying for the six playoff spots that haven't been either officially or effectively clinched.

Statistics and records current through the start of play on Saturday.

Tampa Bay Rays (88-59) : Get swept in New York; slip to a wild card spot

The last time the Rays weren't the American League's "if the regular season ended today" No. 1 seed was on the morning of June 27. However, with just a three-game lead over the Bronx Bombers and a colossal four-games-in-three-days series still to come at Yankee Stadium next week, Tampa Bay has not even remotely locked up that home-field advantage yet. Losing that edge could prove disastrous for a team that is currently 8-2 at home against New York and Boston, but 3-6 on the road.

New York Yankees (85-62) : Aaron Judge never shakes off the rust while Boston ascends to the No. 4 seed

Even before Judge's long-awaited return to the active roster this past week, the Yankees offense was finally showing major signs of life. Since averaging 3.8 runs per game from June 1 through August 22, they've put up 5.7 runs on average over their last 18 games. So, maybe they don't need Judge to be "Peak Judge" to finish this fight. But if he flirts with the Mendoza Line while the Yankees post a sub-.500 record down the stretch, every single good vibration from his return will be long gone heading into October.

Boston Red Sox (80-68) : Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both return, but pick up right where they left off

Houck has been out since last May with a UCL injury, landing on the IL with an 8.04 ERA in his nine appearances. Crochet has been sidelined since this April, making six starts with a 6.30 ERA. But Boston's 2024 ace and its 2025 ace are both rehabbing with hopes of returning in 2026, almost certainly in a relief capacity. Maybe they make it back and become viable options for some middle-innings work in the postseason. The real nightmare scenario, though, would be Crochet coming back a little too soon and compromising his $170M shoulder.

Toronto Blue Jays (73-75) : Comeback quest falls short in painful, tiebreaking fashion

As things presently stand, the likeliest tiebreaker battle for the AL's No. 6 seed would be between Toronto and Cleveland, which the Blue Jays would win by virtue of a 4-2 head-to-head record. But if Cleveland edges out Chicago in the AL Central and the Blue Jays end up tied with the White Sox? Advantage, Pale Hose. Or if Texas finally gets over the hump and finishes strong enough to knot things up? The Rangers, too, would win a tiebreaker against Toronto. And after winning the AL East on a tiebreaker last year, narrowly missing the postseason because of one would be a brutal, full-circle, stomach punch.

Baltimore Orioles (72-76) : Shane Baz loses all three of his remaining starts; finishes 6-18

As a reminder that wins and losses are a rather terrible measure of a pitcher's value added, Baz has actually had a solid first season in Baltimore. Baseball-Reference puts him at 1.6 WAR , while FanGraphs has him at a 3.3 WAR, darn near top 10 among AL pitchers.

Alas, he is 6-15, tied for the MLB "lead" in losses, and three Ls away from joining 2006 Rodrigo Lopez and 2007 Daniel Cabrera as the only O's pitchers with at least 18 losses in a season in the past 50 years.

Trading for Baz just one week after signing Pete Alonso was the one-two punch that made Baltimore feel like a real threat to win the World Series. Routinely providing him with little to no run support is a big part of why they are instead well on their way to ending up with a losing record.

Chicago White Sox (75-72) : Get swept in Cleveland this week; miss postseason

If the AL Central has taught us anything over the past two seasons, it's that it ain't over until the fat lady sings. Detroit had that unreal 31-13 finish two years ago to claim a wild card spot that Minnesota choked away, and then it was the Tigers who relentlessly collapsed last season, blowing what was an 11.5-game lead with 31 games to play.

So, while it has been quite the feel-good story that the White Sox have consistently been in first place over the past two months after three consecutive seasons with more than 100 losses, there's plenty of work still to be done before we can even think about putting them in permanent ink in the postseason bracket.

Chicago has already lost nine of its last 12 and now heads to Cleveland on Monday, where getting swept could be an outright disaster. One would hope they could bounce back and win at least six of their final 10 games against Detroit, Kansas City and Colorado, but they might already be in freefall.

Cleveland Guardians (75-73) : Sputter to the finish line; miss the postseason

Despite a 39-46 record since early June, Cleveland would be the AL's No. 6 seed if the postseason began today. Climbing to the No. 2 seed is still well within the realm of possibility, too. Then again, if the Guardians continue to play sub-.500 baseball, missing the cut altogether is also very much on the table. And if they lose the remaining series to the A's and Royals in the process of blowing it, that would be especially embarrassing.

Minnesota Twins (69-78) : Failed Hail Mary attempt stunts Walker Jenkins' development

Sometimes, top prospects get called up to The Show late in the season and immediately shine, like Sal Stewart and Carter Jensen did last September. Far too often, though, that initial foray into the bigs is a struggle, and you just hope it's something they're able to get out of their system before the light comes on next year. Only time will tell how Jenkins pans out for the Twins, but he is 1-for-25 with 11 strikeouts thus far in September while Minnesota's postseason odds threaten to slip from "slim" to "none."

Detroit Tigers (68-79) : Kevin McGonigle fails to win AL Rookie of the Year

As the Tigers close in on clinching a wildly disappointing losing record—in spite of one of the best run differentials in the American League—there is one considerable silver lining: McGonigle is most likely going to be named AL Rookie of the Year. If that's the case, Detroit would receive another pick around 30th overall in the 2027 draft, thanks to MLB's prospect promotion incentive. However, Cleveland's Parker Messick remains a serious threat to finish ahead of McGonigle, while Boston's Payton Tolle and Chicago's Munetaka Murakami aren't exactly out of the conversation.

Kansas City Royals (66-82) : Play too well; tank lottery odds

Four weeks ago on the morning of August 16, the Royals were 50-74. The only worse teams were the Rockies (49-74), the Angels (49-75) and the Athletics (48-75). Since then, though, Kansas City has gone 16-8, eliminating any hope of having the best odds of winning the draft lottery while moving to within leapfrogging distance of Washington, Detroit and a few others.

It's encouraging to finish strong, especially with younger players like Noah Cameron, Carter Jensen and Jac Caglianone leading that charge. But if it comes at the price of worse lottery odds, it better at least be a sign of what's to come next season.

Houston Astros (75-73) : Collapse and miss the postseason

Perhaps "collapse" is a bit much for a team that hasn't been more than four games above .500 at any point in this entire season. All the same, Houston enters the homestretch as the clear favorite to win this travesty of a division in which the best run differential is a minus-42. The Astros also have three games against the Royals and four against the Athletics, so it really would take a collapse to blow it now.

Texas Rangers (72-76) : A repeat of last September

With two weeks remaining in the 2025 campaign, the Rangers were two games behind the tandem of Seattle and Houston in what sure looked like a race for both first place in the AL West and the AL's No. 6 seed. They proceeded to go 2-11, missing the cut by a six-game margin. Lo and behold, they are once again just a couple games back for both the AL West crown and for the AL's No. 6 seed. Will it be déjà vu all over again?

Seattle Mariners (69-79) : An emphatically mediocre finish to an underwhelming season

Have we officially reached the point where the Mariners—even more so than the Mets—have been the biggest disappointment of 2026? If not, we absolutely could still get there, as Seattle has seven games left against the Angels, three against the Rockies and two each against the Astros and Athletics. It's the perfect opportunity for a miraculous finish to win this division, but also a blueprint for a thorough final reminder of how far they've fallen from last season. There might be fans in the stands with paper bags over their heads for the season finale.

Athletics (60-88) : Putting a Triple Crown on a silver platter

Let's be real: The many-pronged worst-case scenario has already happened to the A's.

They've gone 22-50 since boasting a .500 record in mid-June. Their run differential (minus-186) is the worst in baseball and might end up worse than when they first started tanking four years ago (minus-202). And they just found out a few days ago that one of the top prospects in all of baseball (Leo De Vries) is undergoing shoulder surgery and will probably miss the start of next season.

But the cherry on the sundae would be this atrocious pitching staff gift wrapping some MLB history to a loathed rival.

We'll see where Yordan Alvarez ends up in the AL's batting average, home runs and RBI races heading into the four-game season finale in West Sacramento, but he's already batting .348/.579/.696 against the A's this season. If he's anywhere close to securing the Triple Crown, Jeffrey Springs, Jack Perkins and Co. may well help him get there.

Los Angeles Angels (56-91) : First 100+ loss season in franchise history

Without ever truly bottoming out or rebuilding, the Angels have been stuck in sub-.500 purgatory for more than a decade. As such, their fans were overjoyed with the recent news of Arte Moreno selling the franchise to Stan Kroenke, hopeful that this season will be their "It's always darkest before the dawn" turning point. They are on pace to finish 62-100, which would be the worst record in the club's 66-year history.

Atlanta Braves (87-61) : Squander the division lead after all this time

The last time Atlanta wasn't in sole possession of first place in the NL East was all the way back on April 9, when the Braves and Marlins were tied at 8-5. And not long after, it already felt like this race was over, opening up a 10.5-game lead in late May.

Since having the best record in the National League by a four-game margin, though, the Braves have watched both Milwaukee and Los Angeles blow right past them in the race for first-round byes and have had the Phillies creep up behind them for a possible photo finish.

Even though there is no realistic scenario in which Atlanta fails to reach the postseason, could they mentally recover from slipping to a wild-card spot after more than 160 days in the lead?

Philadelphia Phillies (82-66) : Hit a schneid; miss the playoffs

It's mathematically improbable, but certainly not impossible that Philadelphia could finish behind Chicago, Arizona and San Diego. And if the Phillies haven't effectively clinched a playoff spot heading into the final week of the regular season, insert Ralph Wiggum "I'm in danger" meme here, as they close out the year (at home, at least) against the current projected No. 1 seeds in each league, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay.

Miami Marlins (72-76) : Any more/further injuries to top prospects

We vowed in the intro not to bore you with a bunch of "Star player gets injured" nightmare scenarios, but the snake-bitten Marlins have been without their top two prospects since mid-May when both Robby Snelling (elbow) and Thomas White (shoulder) landed on the IL in the span of a week.

That promising duo was a big reason why Miami was willing to part with both Edward Cabrera and Ryan Weathers in January. The former had just made his MLB debut when he landed on the shelf, and the latter almost certainly would've been in the majors by now had he not gotten hurt. Fingers crossed for 2027.

New York Mets (68-79) : Fall in love with running it back again

Since falling to 43-62 on July 25, the Mets have had one of the best records in baseball, going 25-17 over the past seven weeks. Francisco Lindor and Bo Bichette have both heated up in a big way while the pitching staff has been...well, not good , but less catastrophically terrible. Adding multiple arms is a must this offseason, but the offense has been competent enough that they might largely keep the status quo instead of the scorched earth approach it looked like they were destined to take two months ago.

Washington Nationals (68-81) : Continue imploding; completely forget about the promising start

It feels like a lifetime ago that the Nats were right there in the mix for a wild card spot. In late July, not only were they two games above .500 and one game behind Arizona for the NL's No. 6 seed, but they were just two games back of Philadelphia for the No. 5 seed. They have since gone an MLB-worst 13-28, already breaking the record for most blown saves in a single season while plummeting back into the NL East basement once again. At this point, we're probably back to talking about CJ Abrams as one of the top trade candidates for the offseason.

Milwaukee Brewers (92-56) : Immediate exit from the postseason

You hate to put the "World Series or bust" label on any team.

They've already clinched their postseason spot, guaranteed October baseball for the eighth time in nine seasons. There's a good chance they'll be the No. 1 overall seed for the second straight year. At the very least, they're sitting pretty for a first-round bye.

They've gone 5-16 in their last six trips to the postseason, though, and haven't sniffed a Fall Classic since 1982. And if this year's squad can't change that, it'll be time to start discussing just how cursed this franchise is.

Chicago Cubs (82-66) : Continue to freefall past the Padres and Diamondbacks

Mercifully for the Cubs, there will be no more regular season games against the Brewers. Perhaps that finally stops the bleeding for a team that has gone 11-16 while losing what little faith it ever had in virtually every arm in the bullpen over the past month.

Before that downturn began, Chicago was a mere three games behind Milwaukee for the possible No. 1 seed, as well as 7.5 games ahead of the Phillies. But that NL Central race is as good as finished and the Cubs are now neck-and-neck with Philadelphia for the No. 4 seed—with two NL West teams nipping at their heels.

Pittsburgh Pirates (74-74) : Fail to end the streak of losing seasons

Crashing the postseason party is just about out of the question at this point, but Pittsburgh has a solid chance to post a winning record. That's not nothing for the Pirates, who have finished .500 or better just four times dating back to 1993, most recently in 2018. They spent big (by their standards, at any rate) this past winter to try to win while they have Paul Skenes. And if he had been as good this year as he was in 2024 and 2025, they would be very much in the mix for the playoffs.

St. Louis Cardinals (73-75) : JJ Wetherholt fails to win NL Rookie of the Year

Cincinnati Reds (69-78) : Sal Stewart fails to win NL Rookie of the Year

The situation for both of these teams in the NL Central's rearview mirror is pretty similar to Detroit's: Effectively eliminated from the postseason, probably headed for a losing record, but hoping for an extra 2027 draft pick after the first round if their All-Star rookie can win the ROY vote.

Stewart has 31 home runs, 15 stolen bases and an MLB-leading 107 RBI. However, he has just 2.3 bWAR compared to JJ Wetherholt's mark of 4.7 bWAR , because the Cardinals rookie has some of the best defensive metrics in all of baseball to buoy his modest offensive numbers.

How this vote shakes out will say a lot about what actually matters to baseball's awards voters: Defense and WAR or repeatedly delivering with runners in scoring position.

Los Angeles Dodgers (90-57) : Most important bats never make it all the way back

Per Baseball-Reference , the two most valuable Dodgers in 2026 have been Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages. The former hit the IL this past week and won't be eligible to return until Sept. 23. The latter suffered a hand fracture in late August and might make it back before the regular season ends. But even though we expect both to be available whenever the Dodgers' first postseason game takes place, will they be the anchors of the lineup that they used to be?

San Diego Padres (79-68) : Eliminated from postseason in Game 162

Arizona Diamondbacks (79-69) : Eliminated from postseason in Game 162

It takes two to tango, and what a season-long dance this has been.

Save for the first week after the All-Star Break when Arizona caught fire and briefly pulled ahead of San Diego by a four-game margin, these two have been separated by two games or less—if separated at all—on pretty much a daily basis since Memorial Day.

For four months, they have been ramping up to an epic conclusion: Arizona at San Diego in a three-game series to end the regular season with (most likely) one and only one spot in the postseason up for grabs.

The playoffs officially begin on Sept. 29, but we sure do seem destined for a play-in appetizer on the 27th. And for one of these teams, it's going to end in heartbreaking fashion.

San Francisco Giants (62-86) : Help Dodgers earn the No. 1 overall seed

Not only have the Giants already been eliminated from the postseason, but they are ineligible to draft any higher than 10th in 2027 after earning the No. 4 pick in this year's draft. But with six games still to come against the Dodgers, San Francisco is going to play a major role in determining whether its most loathed rival will be the NL's No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3 seed. Dooming LA to the wild card round would be fun for Giants fans. But losing all six and helping them eclipse 100 wins would be one final letdown in a season full of them.

Colorado Rockies (55-92) : Fourth consecutive season with 100+ losses

While the White Sox have gone from three straight disastrous years to the brink of the postseason, the Rockies remain a hopeless mess, threatening to become the first team with at least 100 losses in four straight seasons since the Mets' first four years of existence (1962-65). Hunter Goodman might get to 40 home runs, but that's minimal consolation for a team with no pitching worth building around.

articles.title: Joey Chestnut Reveals Which Stadium Has the Best Concession Menu Food Items in New Video
articles.summary: The 2026 season has been one to forget for the San Francisco Giants, but they can take solace in something.
articles.body:
The 2026 season has been one to forget for the San Francisco Giants, but they can take solace in something.

The king of competitive eating believes they have the best stadium food in sports.

During an interview with Stadium Eats for Front Office Sports, Joey Chestnut said San Francisco's Oracle Park has the best stadium food.

"My heart still goes to San Francisco a little bit," he said. "They always have good everything, from their garlic fries, when they have brats. I grew up going to that stadium."

While sports fans all have differing opinions about which stadium has the best food, Chestnut's opinion carries a bit more weight.

After all, he holds the record as an 18-time Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest champion and has surely eaten more than most human beings. When he talks about food, people should listen.

And he believes the Giants hold the crown when it comes to the sports world.

articles.title: Justin Verlander's Final Start Before MLB Retirement Teased by Tigers Manager amid Injury Rehab
articles.summary: Detroit Tigers manager A.J. Hinch is still aiming to have Justin Verlander start one of the two games in his celebratory sendoff later this month.
articles.body:
Detroit Tigers manager A.J. Hinch is still aiming to have Justin Verlander start one of the two games in his celebratory sendoff later this month.

The Tigers announced they're honoring the three-time Cy Young winner during their Sept. 25 and 26 home matchups against the Pittsburgh Pirates. The right-hander hasn't stepped onto the mound since March, but Hinch is holding out hope he'll get back out there one more time.

"In pencil, we're aiming for that last weekend, which we know is going to be an emotional, important weekend for him," the manager told reporters Sunday. "But also, if we can get him in that series, roughly on that Saturday, that would be at that seven-day cadence.

"But also, if we can get him in that series, roughly on that Saturday, that would be at that seven-day cadence."

Verlander's reunion with the Tigers made for a great story. He's one of the greatest aces in franchise history and will always be connected to their two trips to the World Series in 2006 and 2012.

However, Verlander landed on the injured list in April with hip inflammation. Detroit then had to scratch him from a June start because of hamstring trouble.

At 69-79, the Tigers are fourth in the American League Central and a long shot to make the playoffs.

If they were in the thick of the postseason race, it might be more difficult to justify starting Verlander when he'd be so rusty. But his farewell is the biggest thing the fanbase has to look forward to at this point. A loss to the Pirates in Game 161 won't mean much in the grand scheme of things, either.

Hinch avoided being too declarative. He said he wanted to avoid making a "false promise" because Verlander's status is far from guaranteed.

For now, one final start from the surefire Hall of Famer is still on the table.

articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cam Schlittler took over the major league ERA lead, combining on a three-hitter that helped the New York Yankees close in on a record 61st postseason berth with a 2-0 win over the Mets on Sunday

Schlittler (14-6) allowed one hit over six innings, his 21st start this year allowing one run or none. The only other pitcher 25 or younger with more in the last 110 years was the Los Angeles Angels ' Dean Chance with 22 in 1964, according to Major League Baseball.

Schlittler's 1.945 ERA dropped below the 1.952 of Milwaukee 's Jacob Misiorowski . Schlitter struck out eight and walked two as Toronto went 0 for 11 against his fastball.

Ben Rice led off his his 38th home run for the Yankees and Austin Wells ended an 0-for-20 slide with a third-inning homer into the right field second deck off Christian Scott (4-5).

Aaron Judge struck out three times and is 3 for 17 since returning Tuesday from a broken rib.

The Yankees (86-63), who lead the AL wild-card race and trail Tampa Bay by four games in the AL East, took two of three in the weekend Subway Series. They were in position to clinch their ninth postseason berth in 10 seasons depending on other team's results Sunday.

Schlittler (14-6) pitched 4 2/3 hitless innings before Brett Baty doubled off the right field wall on his 73rd pitch. Schlitter finished his 94-pitch outing by taking an 111.5 mph comebacker by Bo Bichette off the back of his right hamstring that deflected to Wells. Schlittler walked off the field and went directly to the clubhouse.

The right-hander struck out Francisco Lindor twice on fastballs, including a high fastball for a swinging strikeout in the sixth. He also fanned Juan Soto on a check swing with a 98 mph fastball and the slugger stood with both hands on his hips.

Brent Headrick (76th appearance), Paul Blackburn and David Bednar (34th save in 37 chances) finished the Yankees' 14th shutout. Each team had three hits.

A day after hitting six homers, the Mets were blanked for the 14th time. They are 22-14 since the Aug. 3 trade deadline.

Mets RHP Jonah Tong (2-1, 4.80 ERA) opposes Baltimore RHP Brandon Young (9-4, 3.71) Monday in Pete Alonso 's return to Queens.

Yankees RHP Will Warren (10-6, 4.05) faces RHP Dean Kremer (3-5, 5.65) in the opener of a three-game series Monday in Minnesota .

articles.title: Red Sox starter Payton Tolle throws immaculate inning to open win over Royals
articles.summary: Tolle threw a perfect first inning, just 2 days after Diamondbacks reliever Justin Martinez also achieved the feat.
articles.body:
The Boston Red Sox started Sunday's game against the Kansas City Royals with a perfect note. In the top of the first inning, Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle threw an immaculate inning to begin the game.

Tolle needed only nine pitches to retire the first three Royals and achieve the rare MLB feat: Leadoff hitter Nick Loftin struck out looking, followed by Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone , who both struck out swinging.

Tolle went on to hold the Royals scoreless for six innings, throwing seven strikeouts and allowing just four hits and a walk. Though he found himself in a jam in the sixth, Tolle held on to draw a strikeout from Matthew Lugo and complete the inning.

Boston's bullpen held on in the later innings to win the game 4-1.

Tolle's stellar first inning became just the eighth immaculate inning in Red Sox franchise history, via the Boston Globe's Tim Healey . It was the first for Boston since Chris Sale achieved the feat on Aug. 26, 2021.

Along with Tolle's, there have been only 124 immaculate innings in MLB history; though more rare than no-hitters, there has been an increase in the number of these innings in recent years as pitchers hone their craft and increase their speeds.

Tolle's immaculate inning comes just two days after Arizona Diamondbacks reliever Justin Martinez threw one as well. Five have taken place this year in total, thrown by D-backs' Michael Soroka (March 30), Cleveland Guardians ' Gavin Williams (July 23) and Minnesota Twins ' Taj Bradley (Aug. 25) in addition to Tolle and Martinez.

articles.title: Why I Never Blame St. Louis Cardinals Losses on a Single Player
articles.summary: This has become an issue lately so I’d like to address why you’ll never see me blame a St. Louis Cardinals loss on a single player. I understand why many wan...
articles.body:
This has become an issue lately so I'd like to address why you'll never see me blame a St. Louis Cardinals loss on a single player. I understand why many want to assign blame, but I have some serious reasons why I don't believe in it.

When you think of some of Major League Baseball's most infamous late game blunders, game 6 of the Boston Red Sox /New York Mets World Series probably comes to mind. Everyone remembers Bill Buckner's error as Mookie Wilson's ball went through his legs at first base allowing the Mets to win the game and eventually the World Series. Here's something to consider. Do you know that the Boston Red Sox had 13 hits in that game, but stranded 8 runners on base? You never hear about all of those Red Sox RISP, but Bill Buckner lived with this moment the rest of his life and did it with grace, I might add.

A lot has been made of Riley O'Brien's recent failures to close out games and those blown saves are real and deserve analysis and scrutiny. However, I still maintain that you can't pin those losses solely on him or any other player in the Cardinals lineup. As much as I'd like to forget it, let's look back at the Saturday night game when Riley O'Brien gave up a 2-strike 2-run homer to Randall Grichuk of the White Sox. During that game, the St. Louis Cardinals stranded 9 runners on base. Cooper Hjerpe allowed 4 earned runs in relief. However, it's typical of a closer to bear the brunt of the blame when a game goes wrong. When I mentioned the Cardinals bullpen as being one of the most prominent problems in Saturday's loss, I saw numerous comments on social media throwing hatred at just O'Brien. I will never tell anyone how they should feel about something, but this issue in particular is one I wish fans would rethink.

I have seen some in the past make reference to the infamous Donnie Moore 1986 home run he gave up to Dave Henderson in game 5 of the 1986 ALCS as being key to his eventual suicide. That is a grossly oversimplified story that doesn't really do justice to the struggles that Donnie Moore dealt with in his life. He was apparently a very troubled man that dealt with depression before and after that infamous moment in 1986. One baseball game was not his problem, but it does bring to light the humanity behind all players.

Do I think that Riley O'Brien should be the St. Louis Cardinals closer moving forward? I'm in the camp that says no. Do I think he's the lone problem in many of these late-game Cardinals losses? No way. We can discuss roster construction all day and I'll never get tired of it. I will not, however, be a part of laying blame on a player when a game goes wrong, though.

I cannot think of any baseball game in history that has been solely lost by one individual. I also can't think of any baseball game that has been solely won by an individual. I was always told that you win as a team and you lose as a team. Enough with this desire to scapegoat someone.

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android .

articles.summary: Payton Tolle struck out the Kansas City Royals' top three batters on nine pitches, throwing just the 125th immaculate inning in MLB history.
articles.body: Boston Red Sox rookie left-hander Payton Tolle, sporting one of baseball’s most marvelous mustaches, opened Sunday’s rain-delayed start against the Kansas City Royals by throwing an immaculate inning. Tolle retired the top of the Royals’ lineup on just nine pitches in front of the Fenway crowd. The 23-year-old left-hander attacked the strike zone, firing eight four-seam fastballs and one sinker. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Before delivering his ninth pitch, Tolle flashed an enthusiastic look toward home plate, knowing he was on the brink of an immaculate inning. He then struck out Jac Caglianone to complete the feat. The immaculate inning was the 125th in MLB history and just the eighth in Red Sox history since 1901. Tolle became Boston’s first pitcher to accomplish the feat since Chris Sale in 2021 and the first to do it in the opening inning since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez did so against Seattle in May 2002. EX-MLB SOUTHPAW THOMAS PANNONE DOMINATES FOR NASHVILLE SOUNDS WITH 94-PITCH TRIPLE-A PERFECT GAME The only piece of contact Kansas City managed was pitch seven, a sinker Caglianone barely fouled off toward the left side. The Boston rookie finished with six shutout innings, allowing four hits and one walk while striking out seven on 96 pitches to secure a 4-1 victory. A LAUGHABLY BAD AMERICAN LEAGUE HAS ALLOWED ONE OF BASEBALL'S WORST TEAMS TO CLIMB INTO THE PLAYOFF RACE The seven strikeouts brought Tolle’s rookie season total to 166, putting him second in Red Sox history behind only Daisuke Matsuzaka’s 201 punch outs in 2007. Just 24 hours earlier, Tolle had publicly criticized the modern trend of limiting starters with strict pitch counts. "I would probably consider myself more on the old-school side of it," Tolle told reporters when asked about the decline of starter workloads across baseball. "I grew up thinking that a starter needs to go as long as possible every time ... every time I go out there, I want to throw a complete game. It’s a special thing that is being lost in today’s game." articles.title: Aaron Judge Talks Cam Schlittler MVP Hype, Picks Yankees Star for AL Cy Young Award
articles.summary: Aaron Judge believes New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is pitching at a Cy Young level.
articles.body:
Aaron Judge believes New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is pitching at a Cy Young level.

In fact, he even believes he's pitching at an AL MVP level, as he told reporters on Sunday:

Schlittler, 25, is 14-6 this season with a 1.95 ERA, 0.90 WHIP and 228 strikeouts in 184.2 innings. Winning his first AL Cy Young is probably a foregone conclusion at this point (with apologies to Dylan Cease), but some people within the Yankees believe he deserves even more.

"I think valuable is a good word," manager Aaron Boone told reporters . "He might be the MVP too. I mean, he's been awesome. Just an awesome season."

Schlittler called those remarks "a great compliment" but didn't go into more depth on the conversation. Were he to win MVP he would be the first pitcher to do so since Clayton Kershaw won NL MVP in 2014.

Houston Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez remains the most likely choice for AL MVP, hitting .310 this season with 38 homers, 96 RBI, 95 runs and a 1.016 OPS. But Schlittler has at least made it an interesting conversation.

articles.title: Yankees news: Aaron Boone the butt of Alex Rodriguez joke after showing up with limp
articles.summary: The New York Yankees are inching closer and closer to clinching a spot in the 2026 MLB postseason, and on Sunday, they ended their three-game weekend series...
articles.body:
The New York Yankees are inching closer and closer to clinching a spot in the 2026 MLB postseason, and on Sunday, they ended their three-game weekend series against the New York Mets in excellent fashion — shutting them out 2-0 behind another incredible outing from starting pitcher Cam Schlittler .

After the game, Aaron Boone held his customary press conference, although it looks like the wear and tear of the season has caught up to the longtime Yankees manager. Boone showed up to the press conference with a noticeable limp , and this caught the eye of a few media members, including New York Post's Joel Sherman.

As per Bryan Hoch of MLB.com, Sherman then joked around with Boone, saying that the last time the now-Yankees manager had an injury, New York responded by trading for Alex Rodriguez to replace him at third base. Boone then joked that it's still "too soon" for Sherman to have made that joke.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

As one would recall, Boone suffered an injury prior to the start of the 2004 MLB season — tearing his ACL. With a void at third base, the Yankees then pulled off a blockbuster trade for Rodriguez in February 2004. The Yankees later released Boone as he recovered from injury.

This would end up paying off for the Yankees in a big way. While they would suffer an embarrassing choke job in the 2004 ALCS, with the Boston Red Sox coming all the way back from a 3-0 deficit, they would end up winning the World Series in 2009 — with Rodriguez being an elite fixture for the team at third base.

Boone, meanwhile, wouldn't have too many productive years after he tore his ACL. He did play in the big leagues until 2009, but he was close to replacement level for the final five seasons of his career.

At the very least, he'll always be a postseason hero for the Yankees, as he hit the walk-off home run against the Red Sox in Game 7 of the ALCS, sending them to the World Series.

articles.body:
That's all that remains of a 162-game regular season that started all the way back on March 25, but there is still a lot to be decided in the coming days.

The Brewers and Rays have officially clinched a playoff spot, while the Braves, Dodgers, Yankees, Red Sox, Cubs and Phillies all have at least 97 percent odds of joining them in the postseason field, according to FanGraphs .

That leaves four spots up for grabs, with the AL Central and AL West titles, along with the No. 3 wild-card spot in both leagues still unsettled, and seven teams realistically in the mix for those playoff berths.

Buckle up, it's going to be an exciting finish, rolling right into another thrilling October of playoff baseball.

In case you missed it, B/R's MLB Power Rankings from last week and every fresh power rankings throughout the season can be found at the new MLB Power Rankings hub .

30. Colorado Rockies (55-94) 29. Los Angeles Angels (56-93) 28. Kansas City Royals (66-84) 27. San Francisco Giants (62-88) 26. Athletics (61-89) 25. Cincinnati Reds (70-79) 24. Washington Nationals (70-81) 23. New York Mets (69-80)

A tip of the cap to the Athletics on flawless execution in the role of spoiler last week as they took two of three from the Blue Jays and Mariners—two teams legitimately fighting for their playoff lives on the fringe of the AL wild-card bubble.

The Reds had the toughest draw of any team in baseball last week, facing the Dodgers and Brewers on the road. They finished 1-5 and were outscored by a staggering 59-19 margin across six games, snapping a five-game losing streak with a 4-3 victory on Sunday.

Nationals left-hander Andrew Alvarez tossed seven shutout innings of one-hit ball against the Angels on Saturday to continue what has been a quietly excellent rookie campaign. The 27-year-old has a 2.44 ERA in 44.1 innings since making a full-time move into the starting rotation at the beginning of August, allowing three or fewer earned runs in all eight of his starts during that stretch.

Despite their records, all four of these teams are 5.5 games or less out of a playoff spot entering play on Monday.

The Orioles have the worst record in baseball in September at 3-9, though they did manage to pick up a series win against the Guardians at home last week while snapping a six-game losing streak.

The Tigers went 5-1 last week, including a series win over the Twins , but it's Minnesota who has the easiest path forward. After a three-game series at home against the Yankees starting on Monday, they close out the season with the Angels, Giants and Rangers.

Nos. 18-16: Closer to Good, But Technically Cooked Thanks to the NL

18. Pittsburgh Pirates (75-75) 17. St. Louis Cardinals (74-76) 16. Miami Marlins (74-76)

All three of these teams are superior to the four AL squads in the previous tier, but because the NL playoff race is more competitive, their chances of playing in October are essentially zero. To that point, they are all six or more games out of a postseason berth entering play on Monday.

With their weekend series win against the Dodgers, the Marlins improved to 45-33 at home this season, giving them the sixth-highest home win total of any team in baseball. It's that pesky 29-43 showing on the road that keeps them out of the postseason conversation.

Cardinals catcher Leo Bernal is making a compelling case for a starting gig in 2027 since debuting on Sept. 1 when rosters expanded. The 22-year-old has an .867 OPS with two doubles, three home runs and 13 RBI in 12 games, and he has settled into a spot in the middle of the batting order.

Nos. 15-11: More Than One of These Teams Will Make the Playoffs. Seriously.

15. Chicago White Sox (76-73) 14. Texas Rangers (74-76) 13. Houston Astros (75-75) 12. Toronto Blue Jays (75-75) 11. Cleveland Guardians (76-74)

These five teams went a combined 12-18 last week, as the AL Central, AL West and No. 3 AL wild-card spot continue to be a who's who of middling contenders trying to hang on long enough to punch their ticket to October.

The Guardians and White Sox face off for a three-game series in Cleveland starting Monday, and with just a half-game separating them in the standings, it's one of the most consequential series of the entire season. The South Siders currently lead the season series 6-4, but they have stumbled to a 4-10 record in their last 14 games.

The Blue Jays and Rangers will also meet for three games in Texas this coming weekend, while the Astros play host to the Braves for a three-game set, so a lot could be decided here ahead of the final week of the regular season.

No team has been hurt more by the Padres' recent surge than the D-backs, as their playoff odds plummeted from 54.1 percent a week ago to 26.8 percent following Sunday's action, according to FanGraphs . They face the Marlins and Yankees at home next week, and if they can keep things close in the wild-card race, that season-ending three-game series in San Diego could be huge.

Previous Rank: No. 7 Last Week: 1-0 vs. ATL, 1-2 vs. HOU, 1-2 @ ATL

A six-game winning streak that carried into September pulled the Phillies within three games of the Braves in the NL East standings, but a 4-7 record in their last 11 games has widened the gap back to five games. They are close to a playoff lock, but can't afford to look ahead with the Brewers and Rays still looming in the season's final week.

Previous Rank: No. 8 Last Week: 1-2 vs. LAA, 2-1 vs. KC

The Red Sox are 4.5 games behind the Yankees for the right to host what is shaping up to be a head-to-head matchup in the AL Wild Card Round for the second year in a row. First baseman Willson Contreras returned on Sunday after missing 12 games with a hamstring injury, and promptly went 2-for-3 out of his cleanup spot in the lineup.

The Padres have vaulted from 40.7 percent playoff odds on Sept. 5 to 77.1 percent following Sunday's victory over the Giants to run their winning streak to seven straight. Fernando Tatis Jr. (11 G, 1.190 OPS, 17 H, 4 HR) and Jackson Merrill (11 G, 1.046 OPS, 14 H, 3 HR) have both caught fire at the plate this month to lead the charge.

Previous Rank: No. 5 Last Week: 0-3 @ MIL, 2-1 vs. PIT

The Cubs are now 10 games behind the Brewers in the NL Central standings after getting swept in Milwaukee last week, but a slumping Phillies team still gives them a good chance of hosting the NL Wild Card Series. With a 4.78 ERA in September that ranks 20th in the majors, questions about the pitching staff continue to hang over their October outlook, but the offense and defense are elite.

Previous Rank: No. 6 Last Week: 3-0 vs. COL, 2-1 vs. NYM

With four games against the Rays at Yankee Stadium starting Sept. 22 and a four-game deficit to Tampa Bay in the AL East standings, the Yankees still have an outside shot at the division title. Meanwhile, two more terrific starts from Cam Schlittler against the Rockies (7.0 IP, 3 H, 1 ER, 10 K) and Mets (6.0 IP, 1 H, 0 ER, 8 K) last week might have locked up AL Cy Young honors.

Previous Rank: No. 3 Last Week: 3-0 vs. CIN, 1-2 @ MIA

The Dodgers have reached 90 wins for the sixth straight season, and with four more victories they will surpass last year's win total. Top prospect Josue De Paula made his MLB debut on Sept. 11 filling the DH void with Shohei Ohtani on the injured list, and he went 2-for-7 with a double, a home run and four walks in his first three games.

The Braves' lead in the NL East standings has swelled to five games following a series win over the Phillies, but a tough week awaits as they hit the road to take on the Cubs and Astros. Tyler Mahle has likely secured the No. 2 spot in the playoff rotation behind ace Chris Sale, but the next two weeks might decide who takes the ball behind them, with Grant Holmes the leading candidate for Game 3.

Outfielder Victor Mesa Jr. is hitting .300/.347/.609 with eight home runs in 119 plate appearances since the All-Star break, and his emergence has given a top-heavy lineup another legitimate weapon.

The Brewers became the first team in MLB history with multiple shutout victories in which they scored at least 20 runs in the same season with a 20-0 win over the Reds. They currently rank second in the majors in runs scored (778) and team ERA (3.57), and that balance is exactly why they have now spent six straight weeks in the No. 1 spot.
